theme: Incentive Travel as a Retention Strategy, Not a Reward

linkedin.text:
Most incentive travel programs are built backwards.

The trip gets approved after a record quarter. The destination gets picked two months out. The program gets cobbled together under time pressure. And then leadership wonders why the impact doesn't show up in next year's retention numbers.

The companies I've watched get the most out of incentive travel share one habit: they treat it as a strategic input, not a reactive output.

They define the business objective first — is this about retaining top performers, accelerating a cultural shift, or reinforcing a new commercial direction? The destination, format, and experience all flow from that.

After 16 years of producing incentive programs across 130+ destinations for 25,000+ participants, the ROI difference between intentional and unintentional programming is not subtle.

If you're an HR or sales leader building your 2026-2027 incentive calendar, I'd welcome a conversation about what the data actually shows. DM me directly — or share your current approach in the comments.

facebook.text:
Here's a reframe worth having with your leadership team: incentive travel isn't a perk you hand out after a great year. It's a retention mechanism you build into your talent strategy before the year even starts.

The companies we work with that see the sharpest engagement lifts treat the trip as part of the employee value proposition — not a line item that gets cut when Q3 gets tight.

After 16 years and 1,500+ events across 130+ destinations, the pattern is clear: organizations that plan incentive travel intentionally outperform those that plan it reactionally — in retention, in motivation, and in the numbers that actually matter to the board.
